sec.title: Purpose:
sec.p: Vobramitamab duocarmazine (vobra duo) is a duocarmycin-based, humanized antibody–drug conjugate (ADC) targeting B7-H3, with a drug-to-antibody ratio of ∼2.7. Vobra duo has demonstrated robust antitumor activity in multiple adult cancer models, along with favorable pharmacokinetic and safety profiles in cynomolgus monkeys. Early results from phase I/II clinical trials (NCT03729596) have shown manageable toxicity and promising objective responses in patients with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer. Given the high expression of B7-H3 in pediatric solid tumors, this target is emerging as a compelling therapeutic opportunity in pediatric oncology.

sec.title: Experimental Design:
sec.p: Antitumor activity of vobra duo was evaluated in pediatric solid tumor xenograft models, including Ewing sarcoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, neuroblastoma, osteosarcoma, malignant rhabdoid tumor, hepatoblastoma, and Wilms tumor. Tumor-bearing mice received a single intraperitoneal dose of vobra duo (6 mg/kg) or a matched control ADC (SYD988, anti-CD20 ADC with an identical linker and payload). Tumor progression was defined as a fourfold increase in tumor volume. Event-free survival was analyzed using Kaplan–Meier methods, and objective responses were categorized as partial, complete, or maintained complete response.

sec.title: Results:
sec.p: Vobra duo induced objective responses across multiple tumor types, whereas the control ADC showed limited activity. No clear association was observed between B7-H3 protein expression and therapeutic response.

sec.title: Conclusions:
sec.p: These findings demonstrate the broad preclinical efficacy of vobra duo in pediatric solid tumors and support further clinical investigation of B7-H3–targeted therapies in children.

boxed-text.p: Children with relapsed or metastatic solid tumors continue to face poor outcomes and limited therapeutic options, highlighting the urgent need for biology-driven treatments. B7-H3 is highly expressed across many pediatric solid tumors while showing restricted expression in normal tissues, making it an attractive therapeutic target. Although immune checkpoint blockade has transformed adult oncology, its efficacy in pediatric cancers has been limited, underscoring the need for alternative strategies that exploit tumor-associated immune regulators such as B7-H3. Vobramitamab duocarmazine (vobra duo) is a B7-H3–targeted antibody–drug conjugate (ADC) designed to selectively deliver a highly potent, cell cycle–independent DNA-alkylating payload to tumor cells. In this study, we present the first comprehensive preclinical evaluation of vobra duo in pediatric solid tumor models using a matched control ADC to define target-dependent activity. Our findings demonstrate broad and durable antitumor responses, providing strong preclinical support for the clinical investigation of B7-H3–targeted ADCs in children with high-risk solid tumors.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Despite decades of research, the prognosis for most children with relapsed and metastatic cancers remains dismal (1, 2). Historically, therapeutic efforts focused on the development of standardized chemotherapy regimens, whereas the recent cancer genomics era has shifted attention toward molecularly targeted approaches. Intensification of conventional chemotherapy has yielded only modest improvements in outcomes, often accompanied by significant acute and long-term toxicities. In adult cancers, immune checkpoint inhibitors have emerged as a highly promising therapeutic approach by activating the immune system to kill cancer cells. However, this approach has had very limited success in pediatric malignancies.

There are 10 known members of the B7 family of immune checkpoint molecules, with B7-H3 (encoded by CD276) being one of the four members implicated in interactions between tumor cells and the microenvironment that suppress immunosurveillance. B7-H3 is highly expressed in different cancers and is associated with poor prognosis, which has gained this protein special attention in recent years (3). Functionally, B7-H3 has been shown to downregulate CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell signaling and is also involved in angiogenesis, skeletal system maturation, tumor cell invasion, metastasis, and DNA repair (4). Neuroblastoma cells, for instance, have been shown to inhibit natural killer (NK) cell cytotoxicity through overexpression of B7-H3 (5). Elevated B7-H3 expression, through immune evasion and downregulated T cell–mediated antitumor immunity, correlates with more aggressive tumor phenotypes and poor clinical outcomes across a variety of malignancies (6).

Because of its role in immune surveillance and high expression in many cancer types, B7-H3 emerged as a compelling therapeutic target. Omburtamab, a murine IgG1 monoclonal antibody, has been developed as a B7-H3 targeted radionuclide carrier for iodine-124, iodine-131, and lutetium-177. 124I-omburtamab was studied using convection-enhanced delivery for patients with diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma (7), whereas 131I-omburtamab was administered via an intra-Ommaya reservoir for leptomeningeal disease, with a focus on neuroblastoma (8, 9). However, the FDA rejected a Biologics License Application for 131I-omburtamab in children with neuroblastoma and central nervous system/leptomeningeal metastases, citing the need for data from a well-controlled clinical trial (10). Enoblituzumab, a humanized IgG1 mAb against B7-H3, has been evaluated as a single agent and in combination with PD1-targeted agents, including pembrolizumab, retifanlimab, and tebotelimab (11, 12). Its only currently active clinical trial is an investigator-initiated study evaluating the agent in the neoadjuvant setting for high-risk localized prostate cancer (13).

More recently, antibody–drug conjugates (ADC) targeting B7-H3 have entered clinical testing, including vobramitamab duocarmazine (vobra duo), ifinatamab deruxtecan (DS-7300a), risvutatug rezetecan (GSK5764227), BNT324 (DB-1311), YL201, and others. Vobra duo is a duocarmycin (DNA alkylator)-based humanized ADC (drug-to-antibody ratio is ∼2.7) targeting B7-H3 (14). Valine-citrulline-seco-DUocarmycin-hydroxyBenzamide-Azaindole is a highly potent DNA-alkylating agent, in which cytotoxic activity is cell cycle–independent. Vobra duo is designed to selectively bind to cell surface B7-H3 and undergo internalization via receptor-mediated endocytosis. The ADC is then trafficked to the lysosomal compartment, in which proteolytic cleavage of the valine-citrulline peptide linker by lysosomal proteases releases the duocarmycin-based payload from its prodrug form. Subsequent intracellular activation enables DNA alkylation and cytotoxicity, whereas the linker design minimizes extracellular payload release and reduces off-target toxicity. Vobra duo showed robust in vivo activity across a range of adult cancer models (e.g., breast, ovarian, lung, skin, prostate, and head and neck cancer xenograft models) and a favorable pharmacokinetic and safety profile in cynomolgus monkeys (15). In a phase I/II trial, vobra duo was tested in patients with metastatic castrate-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC), non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), triple-negative breast cancer, melanoma, and squamous cell carcinoma of the head and neck. Preliminary results indicated partial responses (PR; confirmed plus unconfirmed) in approximately 25% of patients with NSCLC and mCRPC (14). A randomized phase II clinical trial in patients with mCRPC evaluated two doses (2.0 mg/kg and 2.7 mg/kg, each given every 4 weeks), yielding confirmed objective response rates (ORR) of 20.0% (n = 9) and 40.6%, respectively (16, 17). Adverse events occurring in more than 20% of patients included asthenia, peripheral edema, decreased appetite, nausea, pleural effusion, diarrhea, fatigue, constipation, anemia, palmar-plantar erythrodysesthesia (PPE, or hand-foot syndrome), neutropenia, and stomatitis. At this time, no additional clinical trials for vobra duo are planned; however, its potential in pediatric patients with cancer has not yet been evaluated (18).

B7-H3 is highly expressed across many pediatric solid tumors, including rhabdomyosarcoma (RMS), Wilms tumor, neuroblastoma, osteosarcoma, and medulloblastoma, whereas its expression is limited in most normal tissues (19–22). Tumor-associated vasculature and stromal fibroblasts also frequently overexpress B7-H3 (23). In this study, we report the preclinical evaluation of vobra duo and a control ADC, SYD988, which targets CD20 and employs the same linker and duocarmycin payload as vobra duo, across multiple pediatric solid tumor panels.

sec.title: Xenograft models
sec.p: Six Ewing sarcoma, 6 RMS, and 11 neuroblastoma xenograft models were tested using the “Single-Mouse Testing” (SMT) design, a screening approach optimized for efficient identification of tumor-regressing activity across diverse in vivo models (24). Of the 45 tumor models evaluated, 8 were derived from established cell lines (CDX; Ewing sarcoma and neuroblastoma panels), whereas the remaining 37 were patient-derived xenografts (PDX; Supplementary Table S1). Five osteosarcoma models, due to their slower growth kinetics and lower rates of tumor regression, were tested with 10 mice per treatment group per arm. Based on antitumor activity observed in the initial phase of testing, additional xenograft panels representing Wilms tumor, malignant rhabdoid tumor (MRT), and hepatoblastoma were subsequently evaluated (25). These xenografts were recently established, and because their growth kinetics were less well characterized, particularly for hepatoblastoma, cohorts of five mice per treatment group were employed to ensure a robust assessment of treatment activity.

sec.title: In vivo testing
sec.p: Severe combined immunodeficiency C.B-Igh-1b/IcrTac-Prkdcscid (SCID) mice and CB17/Icr-Prkdcscid/IcrIcoCrl mice (6–8 weeks old; RRID:IMSR_CRL:236) were purchased from Envigo, Taconic, Charles River Laboratories, or bred in-house, allowing evaluation of drug activity across different host strain backgrounds. All animal studies were carried out per Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee regulations at the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia, M.D. Anderson Cancer Center, and the University of Texas Health San Antonio. Under isoflurane anesthesia (5% in O2 decreasing to 0%–3% via inhalation) using standard procedures, tissue fragments (3–5 mm in linear dimension) were implanted subcutaneously, as described (26). Tumor volumes were measured weekly using electronic calipers and calculated from two perpendicular dimensions. Treatment was initiated when tumors reached a volume of approximately 0.05 to 0.3 cm3. Vobra duo and SYD988 (a control arm, an anti-CD20 ADC with the same linker and payload as vobra duo) were provided by MacroGenics, Inc. and administered intraperitoneally as a single dose of 6 mg/kg. Events were defined as a 4-fold increase in tumor volume relative to treatment on day 0. Time-to-event analyses were performed using the Kaplan–Meier method, and objective response categories were assigned as described previously (26).

sec.title: Statistical analysis of in vivo data
sec.p: An event was defined as the quadrupling of tumor volume from baseline at treatment day 0. The time-to-event was estimated by interpolating between the measurements directly preceding and following the event, assuming log-linear growth. The primary objective of testing was to document the ability of vobra duo to induce robust tumor regressions across panels of pediatric tumor models. The treatment response classification categories used to address this objective were progressive disease (PD; subdivided into PD with and without tumor growth delay, PD2 and PD1, respectively), stable disease (SD), PR, complete response (CR), and maintained complete response (MCR). Responses of PR, CR, and MCR were considered objective treatment responses. Agents that induce objective responses are considered highly active, whereas agents that induce SD or PD2 are considered to have intermediate activity, and agents that produce PD1 responses are considered to have a low level of activity.
The response category for each mouse was calculated as follows:

list-item.p: PD when there was <50% tumor regression throughout the study and >25% tumor growth at the end of the study
PD1 when the time-to-event was ≤200% of the median time-to-event in the control group
PD2 when the time-to-event was >200% of the median time-to-event in the control group
SD when there was <50% tumor regression throughout the study and ≤25% tumor growth at the end of the study
PR when there was ≥50% tumor regression at any point during the study, but a measurable tumor throughout the study period
CR when there was no measurable tumor mass for up to 2 consecutive readings during the study period or intermittently any number of times
MCR when there was no measurable tumor mass for at least 3 consecutive readings at any time after treatment was completed

sec.p: Overall group response was determined by the median response among evaluable mice as follows: Each mouse was assigned a score from 0 to 10 based on their response category: PD1 = 0, PD2 = 2, SD = 4, PR = 6, CR = 8, and MCR = 10. If the median score was halfway between a response category, the group response was assigned to the lower response category (e.g., a median score of 9 was categorized as CR, not MCR). Studies in which the deaths of animals on study were greater than 25% or in which the control group was not SD or worse were considered unevaluable and were excluded from analysis.

The average minimum relative tumor volume (minRTV) was also used as a measure of treatment response. A value of 0 indicated that a tumor was no longer detectable, whereas values <1.0 indicated some level of tumor regression. Changes in minRTV were calculated as minRTV – 1 and expressed as a percentage, with −100% indicating complete resolution of disease and negative values indicating some degree of tumor regression. These data were visualized using waterfall plots arranged from least to best responses.

The significance of differences in event-free survival (EFS) between experimental groups (e.g., treated vs. control) was assessed with log-rank tests. EFS distributions were summarized graphically with Kaplan–Meier and swimmer plots. All statistical testing was two-sided, with a P < 0.05 considered to be statistically significant.

sec.title: Protein extraction, Western blotting, ELISA, and immunohistochemistry assays
sec.p: Xenograft tumor tissues were ground under liquid nitrogen, and ∼30 to 50 mg of powder was used for Western blot analysis. For protein extraction, tissue powder was lysed with ice-cold RIPA lysis buffer (89900, Thermo Fisher Scientific) with protease and phosphatase inhibitors (A32961, Thermo Fisher Scientific). After ultrasonication, the lysates were centrifuged at 12,000 relative centrifugal field for 20 minutes at 4°C. Protein concentrations in the lysates were determined using the BCA protein assay kit (5000002EDU, Bio-Rad).

Equal amounts of protein from each sample were mixed with SDS loading buffer (NP0007, Invitrogen), separated by a 10% Bis-Tris gel (Invitrogen NuPAGE, NP0302BOX), and transferred to Immobilon-FL PVDF Membrane (Millipore, IPFL00005) using an iBlot transfer system. The membranes were probed with antibodies against human B7-H3 (1:1,000 dilution, AF1027, R&D Systems, MN; RRID:AB_354546) and GAPDH (1:1,000, Cell Signaling Technology, 2118; RRID:AB_561053). Proteins were detected with LI-COR IRDye 680RD anti-mouse (LI-COR Bio, #925-68070; RRID: AB_2651128) and LI-COR IRDye 800CW anti-goat (LICORBio, #925-32211; RRID:AB_2651127) secondary antibodies (1:20,000) in a mixture of LI-COR Odyssey Blocking Buffer (TBS), 0.2% Tween 20, and 0.01% SDS. Membranes were imaged using the LI-COR Odyssey CLx Imaging System (Nebraska, USA). The intensity of each protein band was quantified using Li-COR Image Studio software (RRID:SCR_015795) and normalized against the corresponding GAPDH signal. The normalized values were used to plot data graphs (Prism 9 GraphPad software).

VEGFA levels in xenograft tumor tissues were quantified using a human VEGF ELISA kit (ab100663; Abcam) following the manufacturer’s instructions. Tumors were homogenized, and the resulting tissue powder was lysed in ice-cold RIPA buffer (89900; Thermo Fisher Scientific) supplemented with protease and phosphatase inhibitors (A32961; Thermo Fisher Scientific). Total protein concentrations in the lysates were determined using the BCA Protein Assay Kit (5000002EDU; Bio-Rad). All reagents, samples, and standards were equilibrated to room temperature (25°C) before use. Standards or samples were added to a 96-well ELISA plate, followed by incubation with the biotin-conjugated detection antibody and subsequently with HRP–streptavidin solution. After the addition of the TMB One-Step Development Solution, the plate was incubated at room temperature, and the reaction was terminated with stop solution. Absorbance at 450 nm was measured using a SpectraMax M5 microplate reader (Molecular Devices; RRID:SCR_020300).

For immunohistochemistry (IHC) analysis, tumor sections were stained with 1 mg/mL of goat anti-human B7-H3 polyclonal antibody (R&D, AF1027, Lot # HCM422061; RRID:AB_354546). Daudi cells were used as a negative control and Hs700T cells as a positive control in the evaluation of staining intensity.

sec.title: RNA sequencing, bioinformatics, and statistical analyses
sec.p: RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) of MRT was performed at the Greehey Children’s Cancer Research Institute Genome Sequencing Facility following the KAPA Stranded RNA-seq sample preparation guide (KAPA Biosystems) and was sequenced using the Illumina NovaSeq 6000 platform with a 100 bp paired-end module for MRT samples and hepatoblastoma samples (25). RNA-seq data from the Pediatric Preclinical Testing Consortium (PPTC) samples (27) were downloaded from PedcBioPortal for CD276 gene expression (in FPKM units). Gene expression values (in FPKM units) were obtained using the RSEM algorithm (28). Statistical analyses were performed using R/Bioconductor packages. Statistical tests (t-test, Kruskal–Wallis test, and others) were performed using R (v4.1.2; R Core Team 2021).

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Vobra duo was tested against panels for 7 distinctive types of childhood cancer. Testing was done using cohort designs for osteosarcoma, hepatoblastoma, MRT, and Wilms tumor models (Supplementary Table S1). The remaining tumor panels were evaluated using either the SMT design (RMS and Ewing sarcoma) or a design using 2 treated and 2 control mice per model (neuroblastoma). The primary activity readout for all models was ORR as a measure of the ability of vobra duo and control ADC (SYD988) to induce substantial tumor regressions. Another important endpoint was the time-to-event for treated versus control animals, which was only evaluated for models studied using a cohort design. For these models, a delay in time to event that was 2-fold greater than the median time-to-event for the control group (i.e., EFS T/C > 2.0) was considered evidence of substantial slowing of tumor growth. Details of testing procedures are provided in the Materials and Methods section. For each of the tumor panels for which results are presented, Fig. 1 shows objective response results, Fig. 2 shows relative minimal tumor volume results documenting tumor regression using a waterfall plot format, and Fig. 3 shows the median time-to-event using a swimmer’s lane plot format. Details of results for individual tumor panels are provided in Supplementary Tables S2–S8. Detailed efficacy study results are provided in Supplementary Table S9. Kaplan–Meier plots for EFS and line plots for relative tumor volume change for all models tested are provided in Supplementary Figs. S1–S7.

sec.title: Osteosarcoma
sec.p: Five osteosarcoma models were evaluated using a cohort design (n = 10 for both treated and control cohorts; Table 1; Supplementary Table S2). Among these, 3 of the 5 models achieved objective responses to vobra duo, including 2 models with MCR (OS33, OS9) and 1 model showing PR (OS2). A single osteosarcoma model showed a PR to SYD988 (OS2). Furthermore, 4 of the 5 models demonstrated an EFS T/C > 2.0 in response to vobra duo (OS2, OS31, OS33, OS9), whereas none of the models achieved an EFS T/C > 2.0 following treatment with SYD988.

sec.title: Neuroblastoma
sec.p: Neuroblastoma models were evaluated for response to vobra duo and SYD988 using 2 models per treatment group (Table 1; Supplementary Table S3). None of the models showed tumor regression in response to SYD988. In contrast, 9 of the 11 models demonstrated varying degrees of tumor regression following treatment with vobra duo. Objective responses were observed for 4 of the 11 models treated with vobra duo (COG-N-415X, COG-N-480X, COG-N-496X, COG-N-519X), whereas no objective responses were seen with SYD988. Additionally, 10 of the 11 models treated with vobra duo achieved an EFS T/C > 2.0, whereas none of the SYD988-treated models reached this threshold.

sec.title: Ewing sarcoma
sec.p: Vobra duo and SYD988 were evaluated across 6 Ewing sarcoma models using an SMT design (Table 1; Supplementary Table S4). Two models (ES-6, SKNEP1) achieved objective responses to vobra duo, with ES-6 achieving a PR and SKNEP1 achieving an MCR. The SKNEP1 model, which showed an MCR to vobra duo, also achieved a CR to SYD988 and was the only model to exhibit an objective response to SYD988.

sec.title: RMS
sec.p: Vobra duo and SYD988 were evaluated against 6 RMS models using an SMT design (Table 1; Supplementary Table S5). Four of the 6 models treated with vobra duo showed objective responses (all MCRs) (RH18, RH30, RH41, RH65), whereas the other 2 models demonstrated PD as their best response. SYD988 induced MCRs in 2 models (RH30, RH65), both of which also achieved MCRs with vobra duo. Notably, all 4 responding RMS models were fusion-positive (RH18, RH30, RH41, and RH65), whereas the 2 non-responding models were fusion-negative (SJCRHB011_X and SJCRHB013_X).

sec.title: Hepatoblastoma
sec.p: Hepatoblastoma models were evaluated using a cohort design (n = 5; Table 1; Supplementary Table S6). Vobra duo induced objective responses in 3 of 7 hepatoblastoma models, all achieving MCRs (COG891760, COG922822, UTH-0494). In contrast, all 7 models were unresponsive to SYD988. Five of the 7 models (049.FT0921, COG891760, COG922822, UHS-0648-00, UTH-0494) treated with vobra duo demonstrated EFS T/C > 2.0 (range: 1.7–6.0), whereas only 2 of the 7 models (0498.FT0921, UTH-0494) treated with SYD988 achieved EFS T/C > 2.0 (range: 1.1–2.4).

sec.title: Wilms tumors
sec.p: Five Wilms tumor models were evaluated for response to vobra duo and SYD988, with 4 models tested using a cohort design (n = 5) and one (KT-13) assessed using an SMT design (Table 1; Supplementary Table S7). Tumor regression was observed in all models treated with vobra duo (PR or MCR), whereas only 2 of 5 models treated with SYD988 demonstrated regression. Vobra duo showed robust antitumor activity across all Wilms tumor models, with each achieving an objective response (4 MCRs and 1 PR). Four of the 5 models demonstrated MCR exceeding 100 days, and all models achieved EFS T/C > 2.0 (range: 3.0–9.6). In contrast, SYD988 induced objective responses in only 2 of 5 Wilms tumor models (both PRs; KT10 and KT5), with EFS T/C > 2.0 in 2 of 4 evaluable models (KT10 and KT5; range: 1.9–5.6).

sec.title: MRT
sec.p: Five MRT models were evaluated for response to vobra duo and SYD988 using a cohort design (n = 5; Table 1; Supplementary Table S8). Two of the 5 models demonstrated objective responses to vobra duo, both achieving MCR (BT-16 and RBD2), whereas 1 of 5 models showed a PR to SYD988 (BT-29). Among the vobra duo responders, BT-16 represented an intracranial model and RBD2 an extracranial model. Four of 5 models treated with vobra duo achieved EFS T/C > 2.0 (BT-16, BT-29, RBD2, WT-12), compared with only 2 of 5 models treated with SYD988 (BT-29, RBD2).

sec.title: CD276 mRNA expression
sec.p: We previously reported the analysis of the CD276 mRNA expression profiles across many pediatric preclinical models [Supplementary Fig. S8 (top); ref. 29]. This study extends CD276 expression results to the expanded panels for MRT, Wilms tumors, and hepatoblastoma to uncover potential correlations with the antitumor activity of vobra duo (Fig. 4A and B). Among various pediatric cancers, Wilms tumor (FPKM: 27–108), MRT (FPKM: 16–117), and hepatoblastoma (FPKM: 28–69) models show high CD276 expression levels, only following osteosarcoma (FPKM: 17–323) and ASPS (alveolar soft part sarcoma; FPKM: 18–130). Despite the osteosarcoma xenografts exhibiting the highest levels of CD276 gene expression, the overall tumor response to vobra duo in these models was comparable with or lower than that of Wilms tumor, neuroblastoma, and MRT models (Fig. 4A). Furthermore, the OS1 model with the highest CD276 expression across all tumor panels (FPKM: 175) demonstrated a lack of response to vobra duo or SYD988 (PD; Fig. 1A; ref. 29).

sec.p: While Wilms tumors and MRT showed high CD276 transcript levels, Ewing sarcoma models were characterized by lower expression of this gene (FPKM: 5–21), which was also consistent with their lower response to the vobra duo. Because of the likelihood that sensitivity to the duocarmycin payload may obscure the impact of CD276 expression on vobra duo activity, as evidenced by the activity of the control ADC SYD988 for RMS models, we performed exploratory analyses within each tumor type of CD276 expression among responder and non-responder models [Supplementary Fig. S8 (bottom)]. Across all tumor types evaluated, CD276 gene expression showed no clear association with activity, reflected by broad overlap between responding and non-responding models.

sec.title: B7-H3 protein expression
sec.p: B7-H3 protein H-scores in multiple pediatric tumor types and normal tissues have been reported previously (29). In this study, we conducted a detailed analysis of B7-H3 protein expression across expanded panels of Wilms tumors, MRT, and hepatoblastoma models. Wilms tumors, which were highly responsive to vobra duo, demonstrated elevated basal levels of B7-H3 protein (average B7-H3/GAPDH ratio: 3.2–19.7) compared with MRT (1.4–9.5) and hepatoblastoma (0.8–8.3) models (Fig. 4C and D; Supplementary Table S10). Correlation analysis revealed that tumors achieving MCR (n = 9) expressed slightly higher B7-H3 protein levels than those with PD (n = 4; Fig. 4E).

To further explore vobra duo-mediated modulation of B7-H3, we examined changes in protein expression in a “responder” model (BT-16; MCR) and a “non-responder” model (WT-12; PD; Fig. 4F; Supplementary Fig. S9). In WT-12 tumors, vobra duo treatment significantly reduced B7-H3 protein levels by approximately 3–4-fold at 6 hours (P = 0.042) and 5–6-fold at 48 hours (P = 0.025) compared with controls. In BT-16 tumors, B7-H3 downregulation reached approximately 2-fold at 48 hours. The lower basal B7-H3 levels in BT-16 may account for the less pronounced inhibitory effect observed in this model. B7-H3 has been implicated in promoting tumor angiogenesis through the induction of VEGFA (30–32). To evaluate whether vobra duo affects this pathway, we measured VEGFA protein levels by ELISA in BT-16 and WT-12 models (Fig. 4G). Vobra duo treatment led to >2-fold downregulation of VEGFA at 48 hours in BT-16 and approximately 2-fold reduction in WT-12. In contrast, SYD988 did not inhibit VEGFA expression in either model at this time point.

IHC analysis of B7-H3 cellular localization revealed strong membrane staining in Wilms tumors (H-score: 250–290), followed by hepatoblastoma (H-score: 205–280) and MRT (H-score: 160–250; Fig. 4H; Supplementary Fig. S10). Cytoplasmic expression was minimal, consistent with the predominantly transmembrane localization of B7-H3 (3, 29). Notably, Wilms tumors showed no detectable B7-H3 staining in tumor-associated vasculature—an expression pattern previously linked to poor prognosis and increased tumor aggressiveness (33). In contrast, limited vascular expression was observed in hepatoblastoma (H-score: 10–50) and MRT (H-score: 10–70). This expression pattern aligns with the strong antitumor activity of vobra duo observed for Wilms tumors and its comparatively lower activity in MRT and hepatoblastoma models.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In this study, we describe the antitumor activity of the B7-H3–targeting ADC vobra duo across a broad range of preclinical pediatric tumor models. Vobra duo is an investigational ADC containing the prodrug seco-DUocarmycin hydroxyBenzamine Azaindole (DUBA) as its cytotoxic payload. Binding of B7-H3 at the cell surface facilitates vobra duo internalization, followed by lysosomal protease-mediated payload release. Given the well-documented sensitivity of many pediatric solid tumors to DNA alkylating agents, ADCs with an alkylating agent payload like DUBA represent a particularly promising therapeutic approach. The only FDA-approved ADC with an alkylating agent payload is the CD19-targeting ADC loncastuximab tesirine, which has a pyrrolobenzodiazepine (PBD) dimer payload (34). DUBA, like PBD dimer payloads, binds in the DNA minor groove and alkylates adenine at the N3 position (35). As ADCs advance through pediatric testing and potentially become integrated into standard treatment regimens, there may be an advantage in incorporating multiple types of payloads into the pediatric cancer therapeutic armamentarium. This diversification may help mitigate the development of payload-related resistance mechanisms, which can otherwise confer cross-resistance among ADCs targeting different surface antigens.

Vobra duo elicited ORRs exceeding 50% in Wilms tumor, osteosarcoma, and RMS models. Ewing sarcoma models showed the lowest response rate (33%), whereas the MRT and neuroblastoma models had response rates between 40% and 50%. Responses occurred across a wide spectrum of B7-H3 expression levels, with some high-expressing models not responding to vobra duo. Interestingly, the lack of B7-H3 expression in the vasculature of Wilms tumors correlated with a stronger therapeutic response, in contrast to hepatoblastoma and MRT models, both of which displayed vascular B7-H3 expression. Clinical evaluation will be required to determine the threshold of B7-H3 expression required to predict response to B7-H3–targeted ADCs and to identify additional biomarkers of sensitivity or resistance. The experience with the HER2-targeting ADC trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd) highlights this potential, as it has demonstrated significant antitumor activity even in tumors with low surface antigen expression. In the phase III DESTINY-Breast 06 clinical trial, T-DXd showed ORRs exceeding 50% even in patients whose tumors had low or ultralow HER2 expression (IHC 0 with membrane staining; ref. 36).

To distinguish the biological effects of the DUBA payload from those mediated by B7-H3–directed targeting, we employed the non-targeting control ADC, SYD988. SYD988 contains the same DUBA payload and an analogous protease-cleavable linker as vobra duo, providing a relevant control for payload-driven cytotoxicity and linker-dependent drug release (37). The use of SYD988 enables evaluation of antitumor effects driven by the duocarmycin payload independent of B7-H3–specific antigen binding, internalization, and target-mediated delivery, thereby allowing a clearer distinction between target-dependent and payload-driven mechanisms of action in our models.

All 3 RMS models with objective responses to vobra duo were fusion-positive, with 2 of them regressing in both the vobra duo and SYD988 treatment groups, whereas the 2 fusion-negative RMS models were unresponsive. This could be associated with the higher B7-H3 levels in fusion-positive xenografts (average B7-H3 H-score range: 80–160) compared with fusion-negative models (average B7-H3 H-score: 55), although there is roughly comparable CD276 expression for embryonal (primarily fusion-negative) and alveolar (primarily fusion-positive) RMS clinical specimens at the Oncogenomics Data Portal (https://clinomics.ccr.cancer.gov/clinomics/public/; ref. 29). Additionally, the response to SYD988 may reflect the exquisite sensitivity of some fusion-positive RMSs to the alkylating agent DUBA payload.

Among the 6 MRTs, 5 were from patients with intracranial primary tumors, while 1 remaining model originated in soft tissue (liver) (RBD2). However, no consistent correlation was observed between the tumor site of origin and the response to vobra duo in these tumors. For example, RBD2 represents an extracranial rhabdoid tumor (MCR), whereas the remaining 4 models with measurable responses (PD2 to MCR) were of intracranial origin. Similarly, membrane or tumor cell B7-H3 protein expression did not correlate with vobra duo antitumor activity in MRTs. These findings suggest that other relevant factors, such as SMARCB1-associated transcriptional programs, may contribute to the observed differences in response (38).

We observed that vobra duo induced a rapid reduction in B7-H3 protein levels in MRTs within the first 6 hours of treatment, with further reduction at 48 hours. This downregulation is consistent with the known mechanism of vobramitamab, which is internalized after binding to B7-H3 at the cell surface (39). The reduction in B7-H3 levels was accompanied by decreased VEGFA expression at 48 hours, reflecting both the established role of B7-H3 in regulating this pro-angiogenic factor and effective target engagement and intracellular delivery of vobra duo (40, 41). Recent studies in RMS and osteosarcoma cells demonstrated that vobra duo exerts its effect through inhibition of AKT/mTOR signaling, implicating downstream regulation of VEGFA, consistent with observations reported in colorectal cancer (30, 42). The observed correlation between B7-H3–dependent VEGFA modulation and the vascular localization of B7-H3 (i.e., no vascular B7-H3 in highly responsive Wilms tumors) likely reflects coordinated regulation within the angiogenic and immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, potentially driven by hypoxia and endothelial activation. Although B7-H3 has well-documented roles in immune regulation, many pediatric solid tumors are characterized by low mutational burden, limited neoantigen expression, and sparse infiltration by cytotoxic immune cells, which contribute to reduced responsiveness to immune-based therapies compared with adult cancers (25, 43). Our immunodeficient xenograft models recapitulate this low immune activity that is typical of pediatric cancers in general. In this context, VEGFA levels and B7-H3–associated signaling were analyzed as pharmacodynamic markers of target engagement rather than indicators of immune-mediated effects.

Importantly, these downstream signaling effects do not necessarily predict cytotoxic response magnitude, as shown by the lack of a consistent correlation between B7-H3 expression levels and sensitivity to vobra duo across xenograft models. Similarly, B7-H3 expression was necessary but not sufficient for responsiveness to a B7-H3–targeting PBD-ADC (DNA minor groove binder payload) in prostate cancer models (44). Instead, therapeutic response is likely driven by tumor-intrinsic factors, such as prodrug-activating enzyme activity, drug efflux, cell cycle–dependent DNA accessibility, or DNA damage tolerance. Furthermore, we found no clear association between therapeutic response and tumor diagnosis or relapse status. For example, among the 11 neuroblastoma xenografts, 4 achieved MCR and CR, and these responders were split between samples derived at diagnosis (n = 2) and at relapse (n = 2).

Collectively, these findings support B7-H3 as a key delivery antigen mediating therapeutic response; emphasize the importance of identifying biomarkers of payload susceptibility; and further establish B7-H3 as a high-priority therapeutic target across multiple pediatric solid tumors. Consistent with our observations, Brignole and colleagues (37) and Bianchi and colleagues (42) also reported significant antitumor activity of vobra duo in neuroblastoma and RMS preclinical models, respectively. Interestingly, repeated dosing induced a differentiation phenotype in an RMS xenograft (benign rhabdomyoma), highlighting another potential facet of vobra duo’s therapeutic potential (42). In previous work, we demonstrated robust tumor-regressing activity of the experimental B7-H3 targeting ADC, m276-PBD, which utilizes a PBD dimer payload, across a diverse panel of pediatric solid tumors (29). The exceptionally high level of activity observed for m276-PBD may, in part, result from the use of a mg/kg dose exceeding that used for clinically evaluated PBD-containing ADCs (45). Specifically, although m276-PBD demonstrated high activity at 1.5 mg/kg administered weekly for 3 weeks, comparable efficacy would not necessarily be anticipated at clinically tolerable doses in the range of 0.075 to 0.15 mg/kg administered every 3 weeks for ADCs with PBD payloads (46). Our program has also demonstrated high preclinical activity of ifinatamab deruxtecan (I-DXd), another B7-H3–targeting ADC with a topoisomerase-1 inhibitor payload, across multiple pediatric solid tumor models (47, 48).

Although there are currently no FDA-approved ADCs targeting B7-H3, several such agents with topoisomerase-1 inhibitor payloads are being evaluated, including I-DXd, risvutatug rezetecan (GSK5764227/HS20093), MGB088C, YL201, and BNT324 (DB-1311). Phase III clinical trials for one or more of these agents are ongoing for small cell lung cancer (I-DXd, GSK5764227/HS20093, MHB088C), osteosarcoma (risvutatug rezetecan), esophageal cancer (I-DXd), and prostate cancer (I-DXd and BNT324; refs. 49, 50).

In conclusion, our preclinical evaluation across multiple pediatric solid tumor panels demonstrates significant antitumor activity of vobra duo. The comparatively reduced activity of SYD988 underscores the B7-H3–dependent selectivity of vobra duo. Activity was observed across a wide range of CD276 gene and B7-H3 protein expression levels, and pharmacodynamic readouts, including VEGFA modulation and B7-H3 downregulation, confirmed effective target engagement. Although B7-H3 expression enables vobra duo internalization, therapeutic response also depends on tumor-intrinsic factors influencing susceptibility to the DUBA payload. Future studies should leverage multiomics data to define molecular determinants of sensitivity and resistance. Together, these findings support further clinical investigation of B7-H3–targeting ADCs in pediatric cancers, particularly vobra duo in B7-H3 expressing tumors.
